title: Artificial Intelligence for Weed Detection in Precision Agriculture: A Review from Classical Machine Learning to Foundation Models
content: Weeds are among the most significant biotic constraints to global agricultural production, causing annual crop losses exceeding US$48 billion, while the emergence of more than 500 herbicide-resistant weed biotypes has eroded the effectiveness of conventional management, particularly blanket herbicide application. This review, conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines, synthesises evidence from 117 peer-reviewed studies (2015–2026) across five major databases. Unlike prior reviews focused on a single imaging modality or technique, it provides a unified analysis spanning RGB, multispectral, hyperspectral, and satellite imagery together with classical machine learning, deep learning, multimodal AI, and foundation models. Deep learning has become the dominant paradigm, delivering substantial gains in accuracy and robustness over traditional approaches, while Vision Transformers, multimodal architectures, and emerging foundation models continue to advance feature learning and model adaptability. Despite these advances, the translation of benchmark performance into operational agricultural systems remains limited, with fewer than 12 studies reporting end-to-end field deployment. Major barriers include limited cross-site generalisation, computational constraints for edge deployment, the scarcity of large-scale and geographically diverse annotated datasets, and the absence of standardised evaluation protocols. Compounding these gaps, approximately 92% of datasets originate from just four countries, and ethical and responsible AI considerations are almost entirely absent. Six research priorities are proposed: standardised benchmarks, cross-site datasets, edge-optimised architectures, foundation model adaptation, multimodal fusion, and ethical AI frameworks, charting a roadmap toward deployment-ready weed management systems.
